why: Only DecisionLab (22-option threshold) is yes/yes; Laws of UX is partly, and the decoy and expectation sources do not back fewer choices.
Laws of UX and Growth.Design are yes/yes, but both cite the same Zeigarnik effect.
Stanford (citations) and CDC (data source) are yes/yes; the social-proof and credibility sources are weak.
NN/g (costs shown where the decision is made) and Growth.Design (GoDaddy selected-by-default, fear tactics) are yes/yes; GoodUI and Deceptive Design are partly.
Laws of UX and DecisionLab both say attend to peak and end; no primary Kahneman source read.
Growth.Design (Clubhouse 20+ notifications) and Apple WWDC17 (notify only when important) are yes/yes; the PKU source is unreached.
Laws of UX (aesthetic-usability), NN/g (50 ms first impression) and Tognazzini (no loss of learnability or productivity) are yes/yes across three organisations.
Koji (time-to-value benchmark), W3C (context-sensitive help), NN/g (contextual tips) and Apple (remove obstacles) are yes/yes; the Laws of UX homepage has no such text.
Growth.Design (easy asks first), Apple WWDC26 (wait for the right moment) and NN/g (justify sensitive questions) are yes/yes.
web.dev (Rakuten 61.13% LCP, T-Mobile 42% LCP) and WPOStats (three cases on one listing) are yes/yes across two organisations; Amazon's 1% per 100 ms is a latency claim via a third-party blog.
Only Shape of AI (blank-canvas suggestions) is yes/yes; nothing read says to state what the AI can and cannot do or how often it is wrong.
Only Fogg (citations) is yes/yes; NN/g says sources are seldom clicked (weak), Elicit is a vendor self-description, DecisionLab is a memory article.
